  328: @pytest.mark.parametrize("anchor", ORIGIN_ANCHORS, ids=ORIGIN_IDS)
  329: def test_every_zone_origin_is_exact_not_merely_within_tolerance(anchor):
  330:     """The same nineteen points, held to the arithmetic rather than the print.
  331: 
  332:     Each engine reaches its own origin by an expression that cancels to the
  333:     false origin identically - the Lambert's ``R_b + N_b - R_0 cos 0`` with
  334:     R_b = R_0, the transverse Mercator's ``S - S_0`` at phi_0, and the oblique
  335:     Mercator's ``u - u_c`` at the centre - so the result is the false origin to
  336:     the last bit, not merely to a millimetre. Pinned because a defect that
  337:     perturbed the cancellation by a few microns would pass the anchor test above
  338:     while telling us the structure had changed.
  339:     """
  340:     parameters = PARAMETERS_BY_CODE[anchor.zone_code]
  341:     point = projection.forward(
  342:         anchor.latitude, anchor.longitude, ZONES_BY_CODE[anchor.zone_code]
  343:     )
  344: 
  345:     assert point.northing == parameters.false_northing_m
  346:     assert point.easting == parameters.false_easting_m
  347:     # The convergence and scale cancel to within a few ulp rather than exactly:
  348:     # both are evaluated through trigonometry of an angle that is only
  349:     # representably zero, not exactly so. Measured worst over the nineteen:
  350:     # 6.4e-15 degrees (2.3e-11 arc second) and 2.3e-16 in the scale factor.
  351:     assert abs(point.convergence) < 1e-13
  352:     assert point.scale_factor == pytest.approx(parameters.origin_scale, abs=1e-14)

  639:     """A meridian through the projection origin is parallel to grid north.
  640: 
  641:     True at every latitude for the conic and the transverse Mercator, and it is
  642:     the property that catches a longitude-convention defect: get the sign of the
  643:     central meridian wrong and the convergence on the origin's own meridian is
  644:     nowhere near zero.
  645: 
  646:     **The oblique Mercator is deliberately excluded, and the exclusion is a
  647:     fact about the projection, not a gap.** Its grid north follows the skewed
  648:     initial line, so the centre's meridian is parallel to it only AT the centre;
  649:     at 43 N on zone 260001's own centre meridian the convergence is 0.0214
  650:     degrees, and asserting zero there would be asserting the projection is not
  651:     oblique. The centre itself is pinned by the origin tests above, and the
  652:     statewide test below covers the sign along the centre latitude.
  653:     """
  654:     point = projection.forward(latitude, zone.definition.lon_origin, zone)
  655: 
  656:     assert point.convergence == pytest.approx(0.0, abs=1e-12)

  659: @pytest.mark.parametrize("zone", LDP_ZONES)

  662:     zone, latitude
  663: ):
  664:     """Convergence is positive east of the central meridian, in every engine.
  665: 
  666:     The convention lambert.py established and the other two were written to
  667:     match. It is checked here as a property rather than trusted from the
  668:     anchors, because a projection whose convergence sign flipped would still
  669:     reproduce every northing and easting in the lattice.
  670: 
  671:     The oblique Mercator IS included: the 0.6 degree swing across its centre
  672:     meridian is two orders larger than the skew's own offset at these
  673:     latitudes, so the sign still discriminates.
  674:     """
  675:     east = projection.forward(latitude, zone.definition.lon_origin + 0.3, zone)
  676:     west = projection.forward(latitude, zone.definition.lon_origin - 0.3, zone)
  677: 
  678:     assert east.convergence > 0.0
  679:     assert west.convergence < 0.0
  680:

  686: ):
  687:     """Easting increases eastward - the other half of the same sign check.
  688: 
  689:     A convergence sign defect and an easting sign defect are different defects;
  690:     the oblique Mercator's skew means neither implies the other there.
  691:     """
  692:     east = projection.forward(latitude, zone.definition.lon_origin + 0.3, zone)
  693:     west = projection.forward(latitude, zone.definition.lon_origin - 0.3, zone)
  694: 
  695:     assert east.easting > west.easting
  696: 
  697: 
  698: def test_the_oblique_mercators_grid_north_is_not_the_centre_meridian():
  699:     """The fact the exclusion above rests on, measured rather than asserted.
  700: 
  701:     On zone 260001's own centre meridian the convergence is zero only AT the
  702:     centre, and grows on BOTH sides of it - the oblique graticule's grid north
  703:     follows the skewed initial line, and the meridian curves away from it in
  704:     either direction. Measured on this implementation:
  705: 
  706:         43 N  +0.013702587 degrees
  707:         45 N   0            (the centre)
  708:         47 N  +0.013712224 degrees
  709: 
  710:     Not symmetric in sign - both positive - which is the shape a conic or a
  711:     transverse Mercator never has on its own central meridian, where the
  712:     convergence is identically zero at every latitude. That is the whole reason
  713:     the OMC is excluded from the test above, and pinning the numbers here keeps
  714:     the exclusion honest: it is a property of the projection, not a value this
  715:     engine happens to produce.
  716:     """
  717:     centre_meridian = STATEWIDE_ZONE.definition.lon_origin
  718: 
  719:     at_centre = projection.forward(45.0, centre_meridian, STATEWIDE_ZONE)
  720:     south = projection.forward(43.0, centre_meridian, STATEWIDE_ZONE)
  721:     north = projection.forward(47.0, centre_meridian, STATEWIDE_ZONE)
  722: 
  723:     assert abs(at_centre.convergence) < 1e-13
  724:     assert south.convergence == pytest.approx(0.013702587, abs=1e-9)
  725:     assert north.convergence == pytest.approx(0.013712224, abs=1e-9)
  726: 
  727: 
  728: @pytest.mark.parametrize("zone", LDP_ZONES)
  729: @pytest.mark.parametrize(
  730:     "latitude,longitude",
  731:     [(43.0, -86.0), (45.5, -85.0), (41.5, -84.5), (47.0, -87.5)],
  732: )
  733: def test_convergence_and_scale_agree_with_a_finite_difference(
  734:     zone, latitude, longitude
  735: ):
  736:     """Each engine's ANALYTIC gamma and k, against its own mapping's gradient.
  737: 
  738:     The convergence and scale factor come from separate series in every engine
  739:     - they are not read off the coordinates - so nothing computed so far would
  740:     notice if one of them were wrong while the coordinates were right. A wrong
  741:     convergence reaches a sealed survey as a wrong bearing.
  742: 
  743:     The derivation, with no projection-specific step in it:
  744: 
  745:       * A meridian has geodetic azimuth 0. Grid azimuth = geodetic azimuth minus
  746:         the convergence, so the meridian's GRID bearing at a point is -gamma,
  747:         and stepping north gives gamma = -atan2(dE/dphi, dN/dphi).
  748:       * The scale factor is grid distance over ellipsoid distance for that same
  749:         step, and the ellipsoid distance along a meridian is M dphi with M the
  750:         radius of curvature in the meridian - which michspc.spc.ellipsoid
  751:         already derives and tests/test_zone_constants.py already pins.
  752: 
  753:     A central difference over 2e-6 degrees leaves about 1e-7 degrees of noise in
  754:     gamma and about 1e-8 in k, which is what the tolerances allow; the engines
  755:     sit inside it at every point of this lattice.
  756:     """
  757:     point = projection.forward(latitude, longitude, zone)
  758: 
  759:     step = 1e-6
  760:     up = projection.forward(latitude + step, longitude, zone)
  761:     down = projection.forward(latitude - step, longitude, zone)
  762:     d_northing = up.northing - down.northing
  763:     d_easting = up.easting - down.easting
  764: 
  765:     convergence_fd = -math.degrees(math.atan2(d_easting, d_northing))
  766:     assert point.convergence == pytest.approx(convergence_fd, abs=1e-6)
  767: 
  768:     ground = GRS80.radius_meridian(
  769:         math.sin(math.radians(latitude))
  770:     ) * math.radians(2.0 * step)
  771:     scale_fd = math.hypot(d_northing, d_easting) / ground
  772:     assert point.scale_factor == pytest.approx(scale_fd, abs=1e-7)
  773: 
  774: 
  775: @pytest.mark.parametrize("zone", LDP_ZONES)
  776: def test_forward_and_inverse_are_true_inverses_across_the_zone(zone):
  777:     """A lattice of positions round-tripped, well beyond the anchored points."""
  778:     origin_lat = _origin_latitude(zone)
  779:     for dlat in (-0.4, -0.1, 0.0, 0.2, 0.5):
  780:         for dlon in (-0.6, -0.2, 0.0, 0.3, 0.7):
  781:             latitude = origin_lat + dlat
  782:             longitude = zone.definition.lon_origin + dlon
  783:             point = projection.forward(latitude, longitude, zone)
  784:             position = projection.inverse(point.northing, point.easting, zone)
  785: 
  786:             assert position.latitude == pytest.approx(latitude, abs=1e-9)
  787:             assert position.longitude == pytest.approx(longitude, abs=1e-9)
  788: 
  789: 
  790: TM_CLOSURE_BY_OFFSET = (
  791:     # (degrees from the central meridian, bound on the round-trip error, m)
  792:     #
  793:     # Measured on zone 261002 (Detroit) at 45 N, and the bound at each offset is
  794:     # the next round number above the measurement, so a change in the series
  795:     # shows here rather than being absorbed:
  796:     #
  797:     #     1.0 deg -> 5.0e-7 m     4.0 deg -> 5.4e-5 m
  798:     #     2.0 deg -> 7.0e-7 m     6.0 deg -> 1.4e-3 m
  799:     #     3.0 deg -> 5.8e-6 m     7.8 deg -> 1.14e-2 m
  800:     (1.0, 1e-6),
  801:     (2.0, 1e-6),
  802:     (3.0, 1e-5),
  803:     (4.0, 1e-4),
  804:     (6.0, 1e-2),
  805:     (7.8, 2e-2),
  806: )
  807: """How far the transverse Mercator series' closure degrades off its meridian.
  808: 
  809: **This is a property of the method, not a defect**: NOAA Manual NOS NGS 5's
  810: section 3.2 series is truncated, and michspc.spc.tm keeps every term the manual
  811: publishes (its docstring says why it keeps even the ones the manual calls
  812: negligible). Within a zone's own area the closure is at the floating-point
  813: floor; a zone width away it is still micrometres; seven degrees out it is
  814: eleven millimetres.
  815: 
  816: It is measured here because something downstream depends on it:
  817: tests/test_convert.py converts between all 342 ordered pairs of Michigan's
  818: nineteen 2022 zones, and the widest of those pairs evaluates this series 7.8
  819: degrees from its central meridian. That test holds two different bounds for
  820: that reason, and this is the evidence they rest on rather than on a number
  821: chosen to make it pass.
  822: 
  823: Michigan's own SPCS 83 zones never reach this regime - the three zones overlap,
  824: and the widest of them spans about 4.6 degrees of longitude - and no SPCS 83
  825: Michigan zone is a transverse Mercator at all.
  826: """
  827: 
  828: 
  829: @pytest.mark.parametrize("offset,bound", TM_CLOSURE_BY_OFFSET)
  830: def test_the_transverse_mercator_series_closes_less_well_far_from_its_meridian(
  831:     offset, bound
  832: ):
  833:     """The measurement above, run in both longitude directions.
  834: 
  835:     Asserted as a bound at each offset AND as monotone growth across them, so
  836:     the test states the shape of the degradation and not just its size.
  837:     """
  838:     zone = ZONES_BY_CODE["261002"]
  839:     meridian = zone.definition.lon_origin
  840: 
  841:     worst = 0.0
  842:     for signed in (offset, -offset):
  843:         longitude = meridian + signed
  844:         point = projection.forward(45.0, longitude, zone)
  845:         back = projection.inverse(point.northing, point.easting, zone)
  846:         worst = max(
  847:             worst,
  848:             abs(back.latitude - 45.0) * 111320.0,
  849:             abs(back.longitude - longitude) * 111320.0,
  850:         )
  851: 
  852:     assert worst < bound, f"{offset} deg off the meridian closed to {worst:.3e} m"
  853: 
  854: 
  855: def test_the_transverse_mercator_closure_degrades_monotonically():
  856:     """Anti-vacuousness for the bounds above: they are not all one loose number.
  857: 
  858:     If the closure were flat, every bound in the table would be satisfied by
  859:     the same measurement and the table would say nothing. It is not flat: the
  860:     error at 7.8 degrees is more than four orders of magnitude above the error
  861:     at 1 degree.
  862:     """
  863:     zone = ZONES_BY_CODE["261002"]
  864:     meridian = zone.definition.lon_origin
  865: 
  866:     errors = []
  867:     for offset, _bound in TM_CLOSURE_BY_OFFSET:
  868:         longitude = meridian - offset
  869:         point = projection.forward(45.0, longitude, zone)
  870:         back = projection.inverse(point.northing, point.easting, zone)
  871:         errors.append(abs(back.longitude - longitude) + abs(back.latitude - 45.0))
  872: 
  873:     assert errors == sorted(errors)
  874:     assert errors[-1] > errors[0] * 1e4
  875: 
  876: 
  877: @pytest.mark.parametrize("zone", LDP_ZONES)
  878: def test_the_two_directions_agree_about_convergence_and_scale(zone):
  879:     """Each engine computes gamma and k by two independent routes.
  880: 
  881:     The transverse Mercator has a separate inverse series for both (section
  882:     3.24's D and G coefficients, against section 3.23's C and F); the Lambert
  883:     reaches them from the mapping radius either way; the oblique Mercator's
  884:     inverse re-runs the direct equations, which the manual instructs. Where the
  885:     series are genuinely independent this is a real cross-check, and where they
  886:     are not it is still a pin on the two paths staying joined.
  887:     """
  888:     origin_lat = _origin_latitude(zone)
  889:     for dlat in (-0.3, 0.0, 0.4):
  890:         for dlon in (-0.5, 0.0, 0.6):
  891:             latitude = origin_lat + dlat
  892:             longitude = zone.definition.lon_origin + dlon
  893:             point = projection.forward(latitude, longitude, zone)
  894:             position = projection.inverse(point.northing, point.easting, zone)
  895: 
  896:             assert position.convergence == pytest.approx(
  897:                 point.convergence, abs=1e-11
  898:             )
  899:             assert position.scale_factor == pytest.approx(
  900:                 point.scale_factor, rel=1e-12
  901:             )
  902: 
  903: 
  904: def _origin_latitude(zone: Zone) -> float:
  905:     """The latitude a zone's definition is anchored at, whatever it is called."""
  906:     definition = zone.definition
  907:     if isinstance(definition, ObliqueMercatorCenterDef):
  908:         return definition.lat_center
  909:     if isinstance(definition, LambertOneParallelDef):
  910:         return definition.lat_origin
  911:     if isinstance(definition, TransverseMercatorDef):
  912:         return definition.lat_grid_origin
  913:     raise AssertionError(f"no origin latitude known for {definition!r}")

    H1: the three projection engines, dispatched, anchored, falsified
    
    michspc/spc/projection.py dispatches on the type of Zone.definition through
    one table that derives ProjectionKind and engine together - the enum is
    finally read, its stored field deleted (one representation). tm.py carries
    NGS 5 section 3.2 complete with every series term kept; omerc.py carries
    section 3.3 PLUS the centre-variant u_c offset the manual does not have -
    the natural-origin form misplaces Michigan by ~6,969 km, the module
    docstring says so, and the frozen centre anchor discriminates. u_c is the
    module's own forward u at the centre, exact and self-consistent by
    construction. LambertConstants.from_one_parallel inverts the section 3.14
    scale equation; its round-trip self-check is documented as a typo check,
    not verification. convert.py and report.py route through the dispatcher; a
    dedicated pin proves bit-identical constants and results for the three
    SPCS 83 zones, and the 18-digest cross-version pin is green untouched.
    
    Suite 1696 -> 2593, green in pytest and -O, exit codes verified unpiped by
    the session lead. External truth: all 63 frozen beta NCAT anchors reproduce
    inside NCAT's printed quantization (worst N/E 4.994e-4 m vs the 5e-4 bound,
    scale 4.967e-10, convergence 4.707e-3 arcsec), 19 origins land on the
    published false origins bit-exactly, forward-inverse closes at 2.7e-11 deg.
    Manual-side: Table 3.22 S0 for three TM zones to 4 dp, Alaska zone 1's
    seven constants (F pinned loosely per its own printed rounding, proven
    self-consistent with G), u_c = 6,968,872.1107 against the extraction's
    independent 6,968,872.111.

    origin instead of centre (4.8e6 m, 31 tests fail), skew sign (345 km, 42),
    one longitude deviation point each in TM (85) and OM (58), A4/A6
    transposed (22, caught by round-trip and the finite-difference gamma/k
    test). Recorded honestly: the A4/A6 seed moves the frozen anchors only
    1e-4 m because all 63 sit near central meridians - the finite-difference
    test is the pin that actually catches high-order series defects; flagged
    for the interim gate.

    omerc AND lambert from PyInstaller static analysis - all three joined
    LAZY_IMPORTS (the #38 class; lambert was statically visible before this
    change and is not now).

  255:     millimetre of easting is about 1.2e-8 degrees of longitude; the capture's
  256:     own round-trip cross-check measured 5.0e-9 degrees worst over its five
  257:     inverse anchors for exactly this reason. 5e-8 degrees is comfortably above
  258:     that quantization floor and is still about 5 mm on the ground.
  259:     """
  260:     position = projection.inverse(
  261:         anchor.northing_m, anchor.easting_m, ZONES_BY_CODE[anchor.zone_code]
  262:     )
  263: 
  264:     assert position.latitude == pytest.approx(anchor.latitude, abs=5e-8)
  265:     assert position.longitude == pytest.approx(anchor.longitude, abs=5e-8)
  266: 
  267: 
  268: @pytest.mark.parametrize("anchor", SPCS2022_PROJECTION_ANCHORS, ids=ANCHOR_IDS)
  269: def test_forward_then_inverse_returns_the_same_position(anchor):
  270:     """Round trip through our own two directions, at every anchor point.
  271: 
  272:     Independent of what beta NCAT printed: it catches a sign or series defect
  273:     present in only one direction, which an anchor test compares against a
  274:     rounded figure and can miss. Held to 1e-9 degrees, about 0.1 mm.
  275:     """
  276:     zone = ZONES_BY_CODE[anchor.zone_code]
  277:     point = projection.forward(anchor.latitude, anchor.longitude, zone)
  278:     position = projection.inverse(point.northing, point.easting, zone)
  279: 
  280:     assert position.latitude == pytest.approx(anchor.latitude, abs=1e-9)

 1089: def test_the_one_parallel_scale_check_is_documented_as_not_verification():
 1090:     """The k_0 round trip is a typo check; the docstring must say so.
 1091: 
 1092:     Recorded as a pin because the danger is not the code - it is a later reader
 1093:     treating a passing self-check as evidence the mathematics is right, when it
 1094:     is the same equation read in both directions. docs/PLAN-nsrs-modernization.md
 1095:     requires the distinction be documented, so the documentation is what is
 1096:     pinned.
 1097:     """
 1098:     from pathlib import Path
 1099:

 1101:

 1103:     assert "algebraic identity" in lambert_source
 1104: 
 1105:     # And the check itself is live, not decorative: a definition whose k_0 does

 1120: def test_every_definition_type_in_the_union_has_an_engine():
 1121:     """The union in zones.py and the table in projection.py cover each other.
 1122:

 1124:     computes nothing; registering one that is not in the union would leave a

 1126:     cannot be satisfied by an empty table.

 1161:         return ObliqueMercatorCenterDef(45.0, -86.0, -26.0, 0.9998, 762000.0, 1524000.0)

 1301: def test_constants_for_is_cached_without_a_bound():
 1302:     """A bound small enough to evict would re-derive inside one job's row loop.
 1303: 
 1304:     The registry is finite and immutable, so an unbounded cache cannot grow
 1305:     without bound either.
 1306:     """
 1307:     info = projection.constants_for.cache_info()
 1308: 
 1309:     assert info.maxsize is None
 1310: 
 1311:     first = projection.constants_for(MI_SOUTH)
 1312:     second = projection.constants_for(MI_SOUTH)
 1313:     assert first is second
 1314: 
 1315:     # And on a registry zone from the other era, whose Zone record carries the
 1316:     # ``allowed_units`` tuple H2 added. A list there would raise TypeError on
 1317:     # the first lookup; a set would make the record unorderable but still
 1318:     # hashable, so this checks the identity of the cached object rather than
 1319:     # merely that the call succeeded.
 1320:     for zone in SPCS2022_ZONES:
 1321:         assert projection.constants_for(zone) is projection.constants_for(zone)
 1322: 
 1323:     before = projection.constants_for.cache_info().hits
 1324:     projection.constants_for(SPCS2022_ZONES[0])
 1325:     assert projection.constants_for.cache_info().hits == before + 1

 1494:     "text,expected",
 1495:     [
 1496:         # Hand derivations, longhand:
 1497:         #   +01 54 40.49 -> 1 + 54/60 + 40.49/3600
 1498:         #                 = 1 + 0.9 + 0.011247222...  = 1.911247222...
 1499:         ("+01 54 40.49", 1.0 + 54.0 / 60.0 + 40.49 / 3600.0),
 1500:         #   -00 22 23.36 -> -(0 + 22/60 + 23.36/3600)
 1501:         #                 = -(0.366666... + 0.006488888...) = -0.373155555...
 1502:         #   THE CASE THAT MOTIVATES THE EXPLICIT SIGN: float("-00") is -0.0, and
 1503:         #   -0.0 + 22/60 is POSITIVE 0.3666. Four anchors have zero degrees and
 1504:         #   a negative angle.
 1505:         ("-00 22 23.36", -(22.0 / 60.0 + 23.36 / 3600.0)),
 1506:         #   -01 53 16.29 -> -(1 + 53/60 + 16.29/3600) = -1.887858333...
 1507:         ("-01 53 16.29", -(1.0 + 53.0 / 60.0 + 16.29 / 3600.0)),
 1508:         #   the signed zero beta NCAT prints at the statewide centre
 1509:         ("-00 00 00.00", 0.0),
 1510:         ("+00 00 00.00", 0.0),
 1511:     ],
 1512: )

 1514:     assert dms_to_degrees(text) == pytest.approx(expected, abs=1e-15)

  132: def _load_json(path: Path, expect_sha256: str, expect_bytes: int) -> list[dict]:
  133:     """Every row of one NGS file, after authenticating the bytes.
  134: 
  135:     Not cached deliberately: the authentication is the point, and both files
  136:     together are under 1.3 MB.
  137:     """
  138:     raw = path.read_bytes()
  139:     digest = hashlib.sha256(raw).hexdigest()
  140:     assert len(raw) == expect_bytes, (
  141:         f"{path} is {len(raw)} bytes; the capture recorded {expect_bytes}."
  142:     )
  143:     assert digest == expect_sha256, (
  144:         f"{path} hashes to {digest}, not the digest the capture recorded "
  145:         f"({expect_sha256}). The frozen file has changed; re-run the capture "
  146:         f"harness rather than editing this pin."
  147:     )
  148:     return json.loads(raw.decode("utf-8"))

  187: DEGREE_SIGN = chr(0x00B0)
  188: """The degree sign NGS prints its angles with, spelled as a code point so this
  189: source file stays ASCII - the rule tests/fixtures/spcs2022_engine_anchors.py
  190: states for the SPCS2022 material.
  191: 
  192: NGS's file is UTF-8. Reading it under Windows' default code page turns this one
  193: character into two (mojibake), which is why ``_load_capture`` decodes
  194: explicitly and why an angle that fails to parse refuses instead of guessing."""
  195: 
  196: DMS = re.compile(r"^(\d+)" + DEGREE_SIGN + r"(\d+)'(?:(\d+(?:\.\d+)?)\")?([NSEW])$")
  197: 
  198: 
  199: def parse_dms(text: str) -> float:
  200:     """NGS's printed angle to signed decimal degrees, NEGATIVE WEST.
  201: 
  202:     ``45 deg 27' N`` -> 45 + 27/60 = 45.45, and ``84 deg 27' W`` -> -84.45.
  203:     An east longitude keeps its sign, so ``275 deg 33' E`` -> +275.55; the
  204:     caller reduces it. (NGS writes the degree sign itself; it is spelled out
  205:     here only to keep this file ASCII.)
  206: 
  207:     Seconds are optional because NGS's format allows them, not because Michigan
  208:     uses them - all nineteen Michigan angles are whole minutes, which
  209:     ``test_every_michigan_angle_is_whole_minutes`` states outright so a parser
  210:     bug in the seconds branch cannot hide behind never being exercised.
  211: 
  212:     Refuses anything it does not recognise rather than returning a plausible
  213:     number: a silently mis-parsed origin is a zone in the wrong place.
  214:     """
  215:     match = DMS.match(text.strip())
  216:     if match is None:
  217:         raise ValueError(f"{text!r} is not an NGS degrees/minutes angle")
  218:     degrees, minutes, seconds, hemisphere = match.groups()
  219:     magnitude = int(degrees) + int(minutes) / 60.0 + float(seconds or 0.0) / 3600.0
  220:     return -magnitude if hemisphere in ("S", "W") else magnitude
  221: 
  222: 
  223: def parse_number(text: str) -> float:
  224:     """``"1,638,300"`` -> 1638300.0. Every value in NGS's file is a string."""
  225:     return float(text.replace(",", ""))

  229:     "OMC": ObliqueMercatorCenterDef,
  230:     "LC1": LambertOneParallelDef,
  231:     "TM": TransverseMercatorDef,
  232: }
  233: """NGS's ``Proj type`` abbreviation to the definition record that IS it.
  234: 
  235: Glossed on NGS's zone-definitions page (captured 2026-08-28): "LC1 (Lambert
  236: Conformal Conic, one parallel); TM (Transverse Mercator); OMC (Hotine Oblique
  237: Mercator, center)". The record type is what ``michspc.spc.projection``
  238: dispatches on, so this mapping is the link between NGS's word for a zone and
  239: the mathematics MCX runs for it.
  240: """
  241: 
  242: def origin_latitude(definition) -> float:
  243:     """The latitude a zone's grid origin (or projection centre) sits at.
  244: 
  245:     Every definition record has one, under three different names, because the
  246:     three projections mean three different things by it - a central parallel, a
  247:     grid-origin latitude, a projection centre.
  248: 
  249:     It lives in the SUITE and not in ``zones.py``: nothing the program does
  250:     needs it. The extents used to be derived from it, and are not any more -
  251:     they are NGS's own published bounding boxes now - so the only remaining
  252:     caller is the cross-check below, which needs one name for "the latitude
  253:     NGS's ``Origin latitude`` column should equal".
  254: 
  255:     Refuses an unknown record type rather than returning a plausible latitude.
  256:     """
  257:     if isinstance(definition, LambertOneParallelDef):
  258:         return definition.lat_origin
  259:     if isinstance(definition, (LambertTwoParallelDef, TransverseMercatorDef)):
  260:         return definition.lat_grid_origin
  261:     if isinstance(definition, ObliqueMercatorCenterDef):
  262:         return definition.lat_center
  263:     raise TypeError(f"no origin latitude for a {type(definition).__name__}")

  485: @pytest.mark.parametrize("field_name", ["code", "abbrev", "name"])
  486: def test_the_uniqueness_check_fires_on_a_collision_in_each_field(field_name):
  487:     """The import-time check, driven with a deliberate collision.
  488: 
  489:     Anti-vacuousness: without this the check could be a no-op and the registry
  490:     would still import. One seed per field, because a check that only looked at
  491:     codes would pass the abbreviation and name collisions silently - and those
  492:     are the dangerous ones, since the abbreviation names output files and the

  500: 
  501:     with pytest.raises(ZoneRegistryError) as raised:
  502:         _check_zone_identifiers_are_unique((real, clash))
  503: 
  504:     message = str(raised.value)
  505:     assert field_name in message
  506:     assert getattr(real, field_name) in message
  507:     # Both offenders are named. Their shared field cannot tell them apart -
  508:     # that is the whole complaint - so the systems they belong to are what the
  509:     # assertion checks: the message has to say WHICH two zones collided.
  510:     assert real.system in message
  511:     assert other.system in message

  632: ):
  633:     """The behaviour, at the function a job actually calls. Both eras.

  648: def test_a_coordinate_from_a_distant_zone_is_noticed_across_the_2022_zones():
  649:     """What the check is FOR, stated on the 2022 zones as a whole.
  650: 
  651:     Selecting the wrong source zone is the most likely real-world mistake with
  652:     this program. Take each zone's own false easting and offer it as every other
  653:     zone's data: count how many of those 342 mistaken pairs the published ranges
  654:     catch. Neighbouring zones overlap by design - NGS's polygons are drawn to
  655:     abut - so the honest number is not 342, and it is asserted rather than
  656:     described, both to prove the check does real work and to record exactly how
  657:     much it does.
  658:     """
  659:     caught = missed = 0
  660:     for source in SPCS2022_ZONES:
  661:         for target in SPCS2022_ZONES:
  662:             if source is target:
  663:                 continue
  664:             if easting_looks_wrong_for_zone(
  665:                 source.definition.easting_origin, target
  666:             ):
  667:                 caught += 1
  668:             else:
  669:                 missed += 1
  670: 
  671:     assert caught + missed == 342
  672:     # Measured: 309 of the 342 mistaken pairs are caught by the easting alone,
  673:     # 33 are not. The misses are overlapping or adjacent zones, where no easting
  674:     # could separate them and the extent warning is what remains. Before H2's
  675:     # rework the number was 0 - the check was switched off for every 2022 zone.
  676:     assert caught == 309
  677:     assert missed == 33
  678:

  731: def test_every_2022_extent_is_ngs_s_published_bounding_box(zone: Zone):
  732:     """The four extent fields, against ``zoneBounds.json``, exactly.
  733: 
  734:     NGS's page: the latitude and longitude bounds "were computed outward from
  735:     the zone polygon to 0.01 degree precision using floor and ceiling

  737:     checked to a tolerance well inside that quantization rather than to bit

  744:

  746:     assert zone.lat_max == pytest.approx(float(row[MAX_LAT]), abs=1e-9)
  747:     assert zone.lon_min == pytest.approx(float(row[MIN_LON_WEST]), abs=1e-9)
  748:     assert zone.lon_max == pytest.approx(float(row[MAX_LON_WEST]), abs=1e-9)
  749: 
  750:     assert float(row[MIN_LON_EAST]) - 360.0 == pytest.approx(
  751:         float(row[MIN_LON_WEST]), abs=1e-9
  752:     )
  753:     assert float(row[MAX_LON_EAST]) - 360.0 == pytest.approx(
  754:         float(row[MAX_LON_WEST]), abs=1e-9

  774: def test_the_statewide_extent_is_the_widest_and_covers_the_state():

  776:

  806: def test_five_2022_grid_origins_lie_outside_their_own_zone_extent():
  807:     """A grid origin is not a place, and NGS's bounds say so outright.
  808: 
  809:     Detroit's zone is defined about 40 deg 12' N and Ann Arbor's about
  810:     41 deg 18' N - both in Ohio, below the state line - while the zones NGS
  811:     draws start at 41.72 and 41.69 N. Three more origins sit over Lake Michigan
  812:     or Wisconsin.
  813: 
  814:     Recorded rather than smoothed over, because it is the fact that makes "the
  815:     extent contains its own origin" a WRONG invariant to assert - and because
  816:     the disclosed envelope H2 first shipped was built outward FROM each origin,
  817:     which is exactly why it put Detroit's zone extent in Ohio and left two of
  818:     its corners off the south edge of the GEOID18 tile. NGS's polygons do not
  819:     have that problem, and this test is the reason why in one line.
  820: 
  821:     Pinned as a set: an origin joining or leaving this list fails the test.
  822:     """
  823:     outside = {
  824:         zone.code
  825:         for zone in SPCS2022_ZONES
  826:         if not (
  827:             zone.lat_min <= origin_latitude(zone.definition) <= zone.lat_max
  828:             and zone.lon_min <= zone.definition.lon_origin <= zone.lon_max
  829:         )
  830:     }
  831:     assert outside == {"261001", "261002", "261014", "261015", "261016"}
  832: 
  833: 
  834: @pytest.mark.parametrize("zone", ALL_ZONES, ids=[z.code for z in ALL_ZONES])
  835: def test_every_extent_is_ordered_and_finite(zone: Zone):
  836:     """A transposed pair would warn on every point instead of on none."""
  837:     assert zone.lat_min < zone.lat_max
  838:     assert zone.lon_min < zone.lon_max
  839:     assert all(
  840:         math.isfinite(value)
  841:         for value in (zone.lat_min, zone.lat_max, zone.lon_min, zone.lon_max)
  842:     )

codex
The registry cross-check is genuinely authority-facing: it authenticates the two frozen NGS files before parsing them, joins by zone code, and compares every defining constant and bound. The import-time uniqueness and easting-bracket checks also have seeded counterexamples; they are structural safeguards, not vacuous â€œregistry importsâ€ assertions. Iâ€™m moving into numerical falsification and end-to-end job/output behavior now.
Revision and authority are pinned; implementation and tests are now under focused numerical and output-path probes.

  â†’ Audit projection engines, dispatcher, registry, and report/job reachability

  215: @pytest.mark.parametrize("source,target", ZONE_PAIRS, ids=PAIR_IDS)
  216: def test_zone_to_zone_round_trips(source, target):
  217:     """A -> B -> A must return the original coordinate.
  218: 
  219:     Run over a lattice inside the SOURCE zone, so every point is somewhere a
  220:     real file could plausibly contain. Tolerance is 0.1 mm, far below the
  221:     0.001 ft (0.3 mm) the program writes, so a round-trip can never move a
  222:     published coordinate.
  223:     """
  224:     worst = 0.0
  225:     for i in range(7):
  226:         latitude = source.lat_min + (source.lat_max - source.lat_min) * i / 6.0
  227:         for j in range(7):
  228:             longitude = source.lon_min + (source.lon_max - source.lon_min) * j / 6.0
  229:             start = project_point(latitude, longitude, NAD83_2011, source)
  230: 
  231:             there = convert_point(
  232:                 start.target_northing, start.target_easting, source, target
  233:             )
  234:             back = convert_point(
  235:                 there.target_northing, there.target_easting, target, source
  236:             )
  237: 
  238:             worst = max(
  239:                 worst,
  240:                 abs(back.target_northing - start.target_northing),
  241:                 abs(back.target_easting - start.target_easting),
  242:             )
  243: 
  244:     assert worst < 1e-4, f"{source.abbrev}->{target.abbrev} round-trip off by {worst:.3e} m"
  245:

  267: 
  268: # --------------------------------------------------------------------------
  269: # SPCS2022, and the one thing that behaves differently from SPCS 83 here.
  270: #
  271: # Michigan's three SPCS 83 zones overlap, so any pair of them describes very
  272: # nearly the same piece of ground and the round trip closes to floating-point
  273: # noise everywhere. The nineteen 2022 zones do not: Bessemer's low-distortion
  274: # zone and Detroit's are 7.8 degrees of longitude apart, and converting a
  275: # Bessemer coordinate into Detroit's transverse Mercator evaluates the manual's
  276: # section 3.2 series that far from its own central meridian.
  277: #
  278: # **That series is truncated, so its closure degrades with distance from the
  279: # central meridian, and it does so steeply.** Measured on tm.py directly
  280: # (tests/test_projection_engines.py has the table): a forward-and-back through
  281: # one TM zone closes to 5e-7 m at 1 degree off the central meridian, 5.4e-5 m
  282: # at 4 degrees, and 1.14e-2 m at 7.8 degrees. It is not a defect - every series
  283: # term the manual publishes is kept - it is what the method is.
  284: #
  285: # So these two tests hold each POINT to one of two bounds, decided by whether
  286: # the point lies inside the TARGET zone's own longitude extent. No constant is
  287: # invented for the split: the zone's extent is the extent already on the record.
  288: # Both regimes are exercised on every pair, and both bounds are measurements.
  289: # --------------------------------------------------------------------------
  290: 
  291: SPCS2022_ROUND_TRIP_IN_ZONE_M = 1e-4
  292: """0.1 mm, the same bound the SPCS 83 pairs are held to, for a point inside the
  293: target zone's own longitude extent. Measured worst across the whole matrix in
  294: that regime: 3.08e-6 m - thirty times inside it."""
  295: 
  296: SPCS2022_ROUND_TRIP_OUT_OF_ZONE_M = 0.02
  297: """20 mm for a point OUTSIDE the target zone's extent, where the transverse
  298: Mercator series truncation dominates. Measured worst across the whole matrix:
  299: 1.149e-2 m, at Bessemer's north-west corner converted into Detroit's zone, 7.8
  300: degrees from that zone's central meridian.
  301: 
  302: This bound is deliberately looser than anything this program writes (0.001 ft
  303: is 0.3 mm), and it is recorded rather than tuned: it is a **fact about
  304: converting a coordinate into a low-distortion zone designed for somewhere
  305: else**, and a surveyor doing that is outside every zone's design intent. What
  306: protects a real job is the extent warning, which fires on exactly these points.
  307: """
  308: 
  309: 
  310: def _lattice(zone, steps=5):
  311:     """A steps x steps lattice over a zone's extent, corners included."""
  312:     for i in range(steps):
  313:         latitude = zone.lat_min + (zone.lat_max - zone.lat_min) * i / (steps - 1)
  314:         for j in range(steps):
  315:             longitude = zone.lon_min + (zone.lon_max - zone.lon_min) * j / (steps - 1)
  316:             yield latitude, longitude
  317: 
  318: 
  319: @pytest.mark.parametrize("source,target", SPCS2022_PAIRS, ids=SPCS2022_PAIR_IDS)
  320: def test_spcs2022_zone_to_zone_round_trips(source, target):
  321:     """A -> B -> A over all 342 ordered SPCS2022 pairs.
  322: 
  323:     Both ends are NATRF2022, so ``convert_point`` runs the whole pipeline -
  324:     inverse in the source zone's projection, forward in the target's - across
  325:     every combination of the oblique Mercator, the thirteen one-parallel
  326:     Lamberts and the five transverse Mercators. Mixed-projection pairs are the
  327:     point: an error in one engine's inverse that its own forward happens to
  328:     undo would survive a same-projection round trip and die here.
  329: 
  330:     Tolerances per the two regimes above.
  331:     """
  332:     for latitude, longitude in _lattice(source):
  333:         start = project_point(latitude, longitude, NATRF2022, source)
  334: 
  335:         there = convert_point(
  336:             start.target_northing, start.target_easting, source, target
  337:         )
  338:         back = convert_point(
  339:             there.target_northing, there.target_easting, target, source
  340:         )
  341: 
  342:         error = max(
  343:             abs(back.target_northing - start.target_northing),
  344:             abs(back.target_easting - start.target_easting),
  345:         )
  346: 
  347:         in_zone = target.lon_min <= longitude <= target.lon_max
  348:         bound = (
  349:             SPCS2022_ROUND_TRIP_IN_ZONE_M
  350:             if in_zone
  351:             else SPCS2022_ROUND_TRIP_OUT_OF_ZONE_M
  352:         )
  353:         assert error < bound, (
  354:             f"{source.abbrev}->{target.abbrev} at {latitude}, {longitude} "
  355:             f"({'inside' if in_zone else 'outside'} the target's extent) "
  356:             f"round-trips off by {error:.3e} m"
  357:         )
  358: 
  359: 
  360: def test_the_strict_round_trip_regime_is_actually_reached():
  361:     """Anti-vacuousness: the tight bound is not applied to nothing.
  362: 
  363:     If every 2022 pair fell outside the target's extent at every lattice point,
  364:     the test above would be 342 applications of the loose bound and would say
  365:     almost nothing. Count the points that land in the strict regime, and assert
  366:     both regimes are populated.
  367:     """
  368:     strict = loose = 0
  369:     for source, target in SPCS2022_PAIRS:
  370:         for _latitude, longitude in _lattice(source):
  371:             if target.lon_min <= longitude <= target.lon_max:
  372:                 strict += 1
  373:             else:
  374:                 loose += 1
  375: 
  376:     assert strict > 0 and loose > 0
  377:     # 342 pairs x 25 lattice points = 8,550 checks in all.
  378:     assert strict + loose == 342 * 25
  379: 
  380: 
  381: @pytest.mark.parametrize("source,target", SPCS2022_PAIRS, ids=SPCS2022_PAIR_IDS)
  382: def test_spcs2022_zone_to_zone_preserves_the_geodetic_position(source, target):
  383:     """Converting between 2022 zones must not move the point on the earth.
  384: 
  385:     One point per pair - the centre of the source zone's extent - recovered
  386:     from the target coordinates. Same two regimes; measured worst 2.6e-11 deg
  387:     inside the target's extent and 2.5e-8 deg (2.8 mm) outside it.
  388:     """
  389:     latitude = (source.lat_min + source.lat_max) / 2.0
  390:     longitude = (source.lon_min + source.lon_max) / 2.0
  391: 
  392:     start = project_point(latitude, longitude, NATRF2022, source)
  393:     moved = convert_point(start.target_northing, start.target_easting, source, target)

  101: class LongitudeConvention(Enum):
  102:     """Which sign convention the input or output longitudes use.
  103: 
  104:     Deliberately has no default anywhere in the program. The manual and the
  105:     owner's prior MATLAB tool use positive-west; NCAT, OPUS, GPS and every GIS
  106:     use negative-west. Choosing wrongly throws a Michigan point about 340 miles,
  107:     and the two are indistinguishable from the numbers alone, so the user states
  108:     it every run (docs/DESIGN.md section 7).
  109:     """
  110: 
  111:     # The attribution tail ("as used by OPUS, NCAT, GPS and GIS" / "as used by
  112:     # NOAA Manual NOS NGS 5") went at #16 note 2 and #17; the worked example
  113:     # ("(-84.37)" / "(84.37)") went at #28, both at the owner's direction. The
  114:     # sign word alone names the convention completely - "negative west" IS the
  115:     # definition, not an abbreviation of one.
  116:     #
  117:     # These strings are BOTH the dropdown's text and the job record's
  118:     # "Longitude" line, and the owner has twice chosen one wording for both
  119:     # rather than a short label beside a long record entry. The worked example
  120:     # now lives in the dropdown's tooltip, where it teaches the person making
  121:     # the choice without following the choice into every document.
  122:     # Positive west is listed FIRST at the owner's request (docs/DESIGN.md
  123:     # amendment #30). Declaration order is what the dropdown offers, because
  124:     # controls.longitude_combo iterates the enum rather than carrying its own
  125:     # list - so his own convention now sits at the top of it, above the
  126:     # preselected entry he reaches for. Nothing in the program branches on
  127:     # member order; `to_signed` and `from_signed` test identity.
  128:     POSITIVE_WEST = "positive west"
  129:     NEGATIVE_WEST = "negative west"
  130: 
  131:     def to_signed(self, longitude: float) -> float:
  132:         return -longitude if self is LongitudeConvention.POSITIVE_WEST else longitude
  133: 
  134:     def from_signed(self, longitude: float) -> float:
  135:         return -longitude if self is LongitudeConvention.POSITIVE_WEST else longitude

  506: def parse_typed_point(
  507:     first: str, second: str, elevation: str, *, source: str
  508: ) -> PnezdFile:
  509:     """One typed coordinate, rendered as a CSV line and read by ``parse_lines``.
  510: 
  511:     Does no parsing and no validation of its own. ``parse_lines`` is the single
  512:     gate every route funnels through - manual entry, imports and file loads alike
  513:     (docs/method/METHOD.md section 5) - so a typed point is refused by exactly
  514:     the sentences a file row is refused by, and accepted on exactly the same
  515:     terms. ``first`` and ``second`` are a northing and an easting, or a latitude
  516:     and a longitude, according to the job's direction; this function does not
  517:     need to know which, because the reader does not either.
  518: 
  519:     **Every field is quoted, unconditionally.** That is load-bearing, not
  520:     tidiness. A typed field is one field by construction - a text box cannot
  521:     hold a delimiter - and quoting is what makes the CSV reader agree with that
  522:     fact. Unquoted, a typed northing of ``780,000.000`` is split at its own
  523:     comma and the row shifts one column right: it parses cleanly as northing
  524:     780, easting 0.0, elevation 13,221,442.048 and converts without a murmur.
  525:     ``_refuse_ambiguous_grouping`` cannot catch it either, because that guard's
  526:     second condition is a description beginning with a bare number and a typed
  527:     point has no description at all. Quoted, the same text lands in
  528:     ``_parse_number``'s existing grouped-number branch, where genuine grouping
  529:     is honoured and ``1,2`` is refused with the reader's own teaching message.
  530: 
  531:     So the quoting is a semantic decision: it makes ``780,000.000`` *valid*
  532:     rather than silently wrong (docs/DESIGN.md amendment #26).
  533: 
  534:     ``source`` is keyword-only and has no default. It names the row in every
  535:     refusal, and a default would let a refusal describe the wrong column layout
  536:     - telling a surveyor who typed a longitude that his easting is unreadable.
  537:     Callers pass ``TYPED_POINT_SOURCE_GRID`` or ``TYPED_POINT_SOURCE_GEODETIC``.
  538: 
  539:     The optional-elevation convention needs no special case here: a blank field,
  540:     "-", "n/a", "na", "null" and "none" all reach ``_parse_elevation``'s absent
  541:     set, and an explicit "0.00" reaches its explicit-zero branch, exactly as
  542:     they do from a file.

  550:     )

import math
from michspc.spc import projection, tm
from michspc.spc.ellipsoid import GRS80
from michspc.spc.zones import SPCS2022_ZONES, TransverseMercatorDef

def mutant(lat,lon,z):
 c=projection.constants_for(z); lr=math.radians(lat); s=math.sin(lr); co=math.cos(lr)
 L=math.radians(c.lon_origin-lon)*co; e=c.ellipsoid
 S=c.k_origin*c.rectifying_latitude(lr)*c.r; R=c.k_origin*e.a/e.W(s); t=s/co; t2=t*t; t4=t2*t2; eta2=e.e2_prime*co*co; L2=L*L
 A2=R*t/2; A4=(5-t2+eta2*(9+4*eta2))/12; A6=(61-58*t2+t4+eta2*(270-330*t2))/360
 # swap coefficient roles
 N=S-c.S0+c.northing_grid_origin+A2*L2*(1+L2*(A6+A4*L2))
 # easting remains correct
 A3=(1-t2+eta2)/6; A5=(5-18*t2+t4+eta2*(14-58*t2))/120; A7=(61-479*t2+179*t4-t4*t2)/5040
 E=c.easting_origin-R*L*(1+L2*(A3+L2*(A5+A7*L2)))
 pt=projection.forward(lat,lon,z)
 return N,E,pt.convergence,pt.scale_factor

91:@@ -217,40 +248,215 @@ def test_zone_to_zone_round_trips(source, target):
112:+# --------------------------------------------------------------------------
113:+# SPCS2022, and the one thing that behaves differently from SPCS 83 here.
114:+#
115:+# Michigan's three SPCS 83 zones overlap, so any pair of them describes very
116:+# nearly the same piece of ground and the round trip closes to floating-point
117:+# noise everywhere. The nineteen 2022 zones do not: Bessemer's low-distortion
118:+# zone and Detroit's are 7.8 degrees of longitude apart, and converting a
119:+# Bessemer coordinate into Detroit's transverse Mercator evaluates the manual's
120:+# section 3.2 series that far from its own central meridian.
121:+#
122:+# **That series is truncated, so its closure degrades with distance from the
123:+# central meridian, and it does so steeply.** Measured on tm.py directly
124:+# (tests/test_projection_engines.py has the table): a forward-and-back through
125:+# one TM zone closes to 5e-7 m at 1 degree off the central meridian, 5.4e-5 m
126:+# at 4 degrees, and 1.14e-2 m at 7.8 degrees. It is not a defect - every series
127:+# term the manual publishes is kept - it is what the method is.
128:+#
129:+# So these two tests hold each POINT to one of two bounds, decided by whether
130:+# the point lies inside the TARGET zone's own longitude extent. No constant is
131:+# invented for the split: the zone's extent is the extent already on the record.
132:+# Both regimes are exercised on every pair, and both bounds are measurements.
133:+# --------------------------------------------------------------------------
134:+
135:+SPCS2022_ROUND_TRIP_IN_ZONE_M = 1e-4
136:+"""0.1 mm, the same bound the SPCS 83 pairs are held to, for a point inside the
137:+target zone's own longitude extent. Measured worst across the whole matrix in
138:+that regime: 3.08e-6 m - thirty times inside it."""
139:+
140:+SPCS2022_ROUND_TRIP_OUT_OF_ZONE_M = 0.02
141:+"""20 mm for a point OUTSIDE the target zone's extent, where the transverse
142:+Mercator series truncation dominates. Measured worst across the whole matrix:
143:+1.149e-2 m, at Bessemer's north-west corner converted into Detroit's zone, 7.8
144:+degrees from that zone's central meridian.
145:+
146:+This bound is deliberately looser than anything this program writes (0.001 ft
147:+is 0.3 mm), and it is recorded rather than tuned: it is a **fact about
148:+converting a coordinate into a low-distortion zone designed for somewhere
149:+else**, and a surveyor doing that is outside every zone's design intent. What
150:+protects a real job is the extent warning, which fires on exactly these points.
151:+"""
152:+
153:+
154:+def _lattice(zone, steps=5):
155:+    """A steps x steps lattice over a zone's extent, corners included."""
156:+    for i in range(steps):
157:+        latitude = zone.lat_min + (zone.lat_max - zone.lat_min) * i / (steps - 1)
158:+        for j in range(steps):
159:+            longitude = zone.lon_min + (zone.lon_max - zone.lon_min) * j / (steps - 1)
160:+            yield latitude, longitude

163:+@pytest.mark.parametrize("source,target", SPCS2022_PAIRS, ids=SPCS2022_PAIR_IDS)
164:+def test_spcs2022_zone_to_zone_round_trips(source, target):
165:+    """A -> B -> A over all 342 ordered SPCS2022 pairs.
166:+
167:+    Both ends are NATRF2022, so ``convert_point`` runs the whole pipeline -
168:+    inverse in the source zone's projection, forward in the target's - across
169:+    every combination of the oblique Mercator, the thirteen one-parallel
170:+    Lamberts and the five transverse Mercators. Mixed-projection pairs are the
171:+    point: an error in one engine's inverse that its own forward happens to
172:+    undo would survive a same-projection round trip and die here.
173:+
174:+    Tolerances per the two regimes above.
175:+    """
176:+    for latitude, longitude in _lattice(source):
177:+        start = project_point(latitude, longitude, NATRF2022, source)
178:+
179:+        there = convert_point(
180:+            start.target_northing, start.target_easting, source, target
181:+        )
182:+        back = convert_point(
183:+            there.target_northing, there.target_easting, target, source
184:+        )
185:+
186:+        error = max(
187:+            abs(back.target_northing - start.target_northing),
188:+            abs(back.target_easting - start.target_easting),
189:+        )
190:+
191:+        in_zone = target.lon_min <= longitude <= target.lon_max
192:+        bound = (
193:+            SPCS2022_ROUND_TRIP_IN_ZONE_M
194:+            if in_zone
195:+            else SPCS2022_ROUND_TRIP_OUT_OF_ZONE_M
196:+        )
197:+        assert error < bound, (
198:+            f"{source.abbrev}->{target.abbrev} at {latitude}, {longitude} "
199:+            f"({'inside' if in_zone else 'outside'} the target's extent) "
200:+            f"round-trips off by {error:.3e} m"
201:+        )
202:+

204:+def test_the_strict_round_trip_regime_is_actually_reached():
205:+    """Anti-vacuousness: the tight bound is not applied to nothing.
206:+
207:+    If every 2022 pair fell outside the target's extent at every lattice point,
208:+    the test above would be 342 applications of the loose bound and would say
209:+    almost nothing. Count the points that land in the strict regime, and assert
210:+    both regimes are populated.
211:+    """
212:+    strict = loose = 0
213:+    for source, target in SPCS2022_PAIRS:
214:+        for _latitude, longitude in _lattice(source):
215:+            if target.lon_min <= longitude <= target.lon_max:
216:+                strict += 1
217:+            else:
218:+                loose += 1
219:+
220:+    assert strict > 0 and loose > 0
221:+    # 342 pairs x 25 lattice points = 8,550 checks in all.
222:+    assert strict + loose == 342 * 25

# CLAUDE.md â€” MCX (Martin Coordinate Exchange)

A Windows desktop tool that converts survey coordinate files between the three
Michigan State Plane Coordinate System of 1983 zones, and between State Plane
and geodetic positions. It is used by a licensed professional surveyor to move
job coordinates across zone boundaries. **A wrong coordinate here lands on a
sealed survey or a recorded legal description and moves a boundary.** That
sentence calibrates everything below.

**Read `docs/DESIGN.md` before any engineering change.** It is the design source
of truth; this file is the working summary. The standing method is
`docs/method/METHOD.md` â€” defaults, not law; record deviations in the DESIGN.md
amendment log.

## What it is

Reads a PNEZD coordinate file (point, northing, easting, elevation,
description â€” no header row), converts it from one Michigan zone to another, and
writes three files: a clean PNEZD export for CAD, a full-audit CSV, and a
plain-text job record. Also converts geodetic â‡„ State Plane in either direction.
Reports grid scale factor, convergence angle, elevation factor and combined
factor per point, with geoid separation from a bundled GEOID18 grid.

It deliberately does **not** do UTM, SPCS2022, NAD 83 â†” NATRF2022
transformation, other states, NAD 27, or two-point azimuth/distance. See
DESIGN.md Â§10 for why each was deferred.

### The finding that changed the plan, and the one still open

**Plan Â§2.5 is superseded (Â§2.5a).** It said `.trn` is biquadratic and `.err`
bilinear, and asked for a pin that fails if the two are unified. **That pin would
have enshrined a defect.** `ngs_grid.interpolate_biquadratic` anchors its 3Ã—3
stencil at `int(row) - 1`, off-centre; both VERTCON grids want it centred on the
nearest node. Then both are biquadratic and both land at **0.47 mm** against NCAT,
20/20 exact, where the old scheme reaches 8.46 mm. **Verified bit-identical to
NOAA's own published algorithm** â€” `Vertcon.java`'s `getGridRow` transcribed
literally, max difference exactly 0.0 over 18,000 positions.

**DESIGN.md #8 is corrected.** It said NGS does not document INTG's scheme. NGS
does: NOAA TM NOS NGS-84, and `intg.f` anchors with `nint()` â€” nearest node. So
**GEOID18's anchoring is not INTG's**, a claim three docstrings and the 0.1.0
release notes carried.

**OWNER'S INSTRUCTION, 2026-08-07: replicate NOAA as closely as possible, they
are the authority.** That decides the open question â€” **GEOID18 is to be
re-anchored to nearest-node**, as its own work package, because it touches
released code and needs its own discriminating anchors (the existing 20 cannot
tell the schemes apart; 120 points sampled where they diverge give floor rms
0.715 mm against nearest-node 0.454). Cost of the current anchoring is ~4 mm in a
*reported geoid separation* and ~6e-10 in an elevation factor â€” **no coordinate
moves** â€” which is why it was not folded into a vertical-datum build.

**STILL OPEN, and it is a disclosure decision for WP-V7:** the `.err` grid
interpolates **negative** at ~0.43% of Michigan positions (956 of 223,850 sampled,
worst âˆ’0.027 m). A negative one-sigma is not a quantity. **NOAA's own published
code produces the same negatives; NOAA's live NCAT service returns a positive
value there** (+0.011 m where we compute âˆ’0.00965 m), and no rule maps one to the
other â€” not `abs()`, not clamping. So `sigma_m` **refuses**, `modeled_error_raw_m`
keeps the raw value readable under a name that cannot be mistaken for an
uncertainty, and **the shift is unaffected and still reported**. All three
paper-overs are pinned as failures.

### Next build, when it comes

- **NGVD 29 â†’ NAVD 88 â€” THIS IS THE NEXT BUILD, and it is now PLANNED: see
  `docs/PLAN-vertical-datums.md` and the status section at the top of this file.**
  Owner's decision at the close of 0.3.0 (DESIGN.md **#32**); sizing is #22 and
  stands as written â€” the V0 gate confirmed #22's data claims in every
  particular. MEDIUM, every input available today. Build the **vertical-transformation
  registry keyed by (source, target)** rather than one hard-wired path, because
  that registry is how NAPGD2022 later arrives as data. Two risks, neither about
  effort: disclosing a *modeled* shift inside a number that looks exact, and the
  `trn` grid's sign/direction semantics â€” the defect class this project has
  already been burned by.
- **NAPGD2022, after it** â€” blocked on NGS, not on us (#22). **Backwards
  compatibility is a requirement, not an assumption:** it does not retire
  NAVD 88 or NGVD 29. A job converted in 2026 must still convert and still
  reproduce afterwards, so the registry keeps every pair it has carried,
  elevations stay datum-tagged, the datum in force is named in every output, and
  an unestablished datum refuses rather than assuming the newest.
- **SPCS2022 â€” not next, and DOWNSTREAM OF NAPGD2022, not parallel to it.** The
  modernized NSRS has two halves that arrive together: SPCS2022 coordinates are
  defined on **NATRF2022**, and **NAPGD2022** is the geopotential half
  (GEOID2022 replacing GEOID18 and NAVD 88). This program reports elevation and
  combined factors, so an SPCS2022 point carrying a GEOID18/NAVD 88 factor mixes
  two eras inside one number â€” and 18 of Michigan's 19 zones are LDPs designed
  at a topographic height, where the height side is load-bearing. So the order
  above is a dependency order. Spec is #21; its own blockers are unchanged â€” no
  official NAD83(2011)â†’NATRF2022 transformation, and the transverse and oblique
  Mercator engines this program does not have.
- **Rename durability** (#23) â€” if it is ever worth it, `MoveFileEx` with
  `MOVEFILE_WRITE_THROUGH` via `ctypes`.

## Repo layout

```
michspc/spc/      computation core â€” stdlib only; no Qt, no file I/O, no network
michspc/fileio/   readers and writers; the ONLY layer that touches csv or the
                  NGS binary grids. Named fileio, never io (shadows stdlib).
michspc/gui/      PySide6; never computes a domain result
tests/            suite; every expected value hand-derived in a comment
data/             four NGS grids, unmodified, each SHA-256 pinned: g2018u3.bin,
                  g2012bu3.bin, and the VERTCON 3.0 .trn/.err pair
review/           committed review harnesses and captured NGS truth (#36)
docs/             DESIGN.md (authority), method/, the NOAA manual, reference/
```

## Non-negotiable conventions (enforce in review)

- Units explicit at every boundary; International feet is the default because
  Michigan legislated it, and the unit in force is stated in every output file.
- Longitude sign convention: **no default in the core** â€” `JobSettings`
  requires it and `job.run` refuses a geodetic job without it. The GUI dropdown
  opens on positive-west (DESIGN.md #29, owner's instruction); that is a
  decision, not a regression, and #29 says why.
- Fail closed, never fabricate; refusals name the offending item.
- Missing elevation writes `N/A` in factor columns â€” never `1.0`.
- One authoritative representation per fact; derived values are never stored.
- One entry point per data path; loaders validate as strictly as the UI.
- No uncited constants â€” document and page, in an adjacent comment.
- Exports never silently clobber; atomic stage-and-rename.
- No load-bearing asserts in production code; the suite runs under `-O`.
- Cross-frame conversion refuses loudly. Never a silent pass-through.
- The rigorous Â§3.1 Lambert equations are the only computation path. What
  verifies them is external and lives in the suite: the frozen NGS NCAT anchors
  and the published Appendix C constants (DESIGN.md #14).

## Development process

Work packages by subagents â†’ session lead independently re-derives load-bearing
math before accepting â†’ independent adversarial review (Codex CLI) at the build
midpoint AND at closing â†’ fix at the root, pin each finding with the reviewer's
own counterexample, falsify the pin, then narrowing re-confirmation until
approved. Commit per gated milestone; push after gates. Suite green in both
`pytest` and `-O` modes before any commit.

+# --------------------------------------------------------------------------
+# The INVERSE side's derivative. Every engine, no exemptions.

+# Until the interim H1+H2 gate there was no derivative check on any inverse at
+# all: test_convergence_and_scale_agree_with_a_finite_difference differentiates
+# the FORWARD mapping only. The gate demonstrated what that costs by seeding the
+# inverse's B7 denominator 5040 -> 5000 and watching 1,674 tests stay green.
+#
+# The check here is the composition rule. If ``inverse`` really is the inverse
+# of ``forward``, then the Jacobian of one is the matrix inverse of the other's
+# at the same point, so their product is the identity:
+#
+#     J_inv = [[d phi / dN, d phi / dE],      J_fwd = [[dN / d phi, dN / d lam],
+#              [d lam / dN, d lam / dE]]               [dE / d phi, dE / d lam]]
+#
+#     J_inv . J_fwd = I
+#
+# Both are taken by central difference on the real public entry points, so no
+# engine internals are touched and the test reads the same for all four
+# projections. The product is dimensionless, which is what lets one tolerance
+# cover engines whose coordinates are metres and whose positions are degrees.
+#
+# **All four entries are asserted separately.** That is the same lesson the
+# closure table above carries: collapsing them with max() lets the entry with
+# the larger legitimate truncation hide a defect in another.
+# --------------------------------------------------------------------------
+
+JACOBIAN_FORWARD_STEP_DEG = 1e-4
+JACOBIAN_INVERSE_STEP_M = 10.0
+"""Central-difference steps, chosen where truncation and round-off cross.
+
+For the forward step: truncation goes as h^2/6 times the third derivative,
+about 5e-13 relative at 1e-4 degrees; round-off goes as the ulp of a
+million-metre coordinate divided by 2h, about 1e-11 relative. For the inverse
+step: the same two terms at 10 m give about 4e-13 and 6e-11. Both are
+round-off-dominated, and both are near the minimum - measured on an
+exact-inverse engine (LC1 261017, 7.8 degrees off its meridian), the worst
+product entry is 1.0e-10 at (1e-3, 100 m), 6.0e-11 at these steps, and
+1.1e-09 at (1e-5, 1 m), so a ten-times-smaller step is ten times WORSE.
+"""
+
+JACOBIAN_TOLERANCE = 5e-9
+"""How far a product entry may sit from its pinned value.
+
+Derived from the finite-difference noise above, not fitted: the worst entry
+measured on any engine whose inverse is exact - both Lamberts and the oblique
+Mercator, at both probes - is 1.04e-10, so this is about fifty times the
+measured noise floor. It is deliberately ONE absolute number for every entry of
+every engine, so that a pinned truncation value and a pinned zero are held to
+the same standard and no engine gets a tolerance of its own.
+"""

+def _jacobian_forward(latitude, longitude, zone):
+    """[[dN/dphi, dN/dlam], [dE/dphi, dE/dlam]], metres per degree."""
+    step = JACOBIAN_FORWARD_STEP_DEG
+    north = projection.forward(latitude + step, longitude, zone)
+    south = projection.forward(latitude - step, longitude, zone)
+    east = projection.forward(latitude, longitude + step, zone)
+    west = projection.forward(latitude, longitude - step, zone)
+    return (
+        (north.northing - south.northing) / (2.0 * step),
+        (east.northing - west.northing) / (2.0 * step),
+        (north.easting - south.easting) / (2.0 * step),
+        (east.easting - west.easting) / (2.0 * step),
+    )
+
+
+def _jacobian_inverse(northing, easting, zone):
+    """[[dphi/dN, dphi/dE], [dlam/dN, dlam/dE]], degrees per metre."""
+    step = JACOBIAN_INVERSE_STEP_M
+    up = projection.inverse(northing + step, easting, zone)
+    down = projection.inverse(northing - step, easting, zone)
+    right = projection.inverse(northing, easting + step, zone)
+    left = projection.inverse(northing, easting - step, zone)
+    return (
+        (up.latitude - down.latitude) / (2.0 * step),
+        (right.latitude - left.latitude) / (2.0 * step),
+        (up.longitude - down.longitude) / (2.0 * step),
+        (right.longitude - left.longitude) / (2.0 * step),
+    )
+
+
+def _jacobian_product_minus_identity(latitude, longitude, zone):
+    """J_inv . J_fwd - I, as four numbers in reading order."""
+    point = projection.forward(latitude, longitude, zone)
+    f11, f12, f21, f22 = _jacobian_forward(latitude, longitude, zone)
+    g11, g12, g21, g22 = _jacobian_inverse(point.northing, point.easting, zone)
+    return (
+        g11 * f11 + g12 * f21 - 1.0,
+        g11 * f12 + g12 * f22,
+        g21 * f11 + g22 * f21,
+        g21 * f12 + g22 * f22 - 1.0,
+    )

+def test_the_jacobian_check_would_notice_a_broken_inverse():

+point of this table.** An earlier version stored one bound per offset on

+numbers above: at every offset the LATITUDE residual is four to seven times the
+longitude residual, and B7 belongs to the longitude series alone. Taking the
+max threw away the only component that carried the defect. Under that seed the
+longitude column reads 3.9e-12 / 1.6e-10 / 5.9e-09 / 5.6e-08 at 3, 4, 6 and 7.8

+column is unchanged to every digit.
+
+Tolerance: 1% relative, or 1e-11 degrees absolute, whichever is larger
+(``pytest.approx`` takes the looser of the two). The absolute floor is the
+round-off floor of these coordinates - a double holds 45 degrees to about
+7e-15, and the accumulated round-off of the two series is a few thousand ulps,
+which is what the 1 and 2 degree rows are showing rather than any truncation.
+Above 3 degrees the values are truncation-dominated and the 1% band is what
+makes a coefficient change move the curve and fail.

+def _captured_convergence(text: str) -> str:
+    """A captured convergence string in the form the fixture stores it in.
+
+    ``"+01 deg 54 prime 40.49 double-prime"`` -> ``"+01 54 40.49"``. Only the
+    three glyphs are removed and the whitespace is renormalised; every digit and

+    fixture's docstring documents.

+            f"E {row['easting_m']}) and the fixture does not"

 """Tolerances, each derived from the precision beta NCAT printed - never chosen
 to make a test pass. A printed figure cannot be held to more than half a unit in
 its last place, and holding it to less would let a real error hide."""
 
 
 def dms_to_degrees(text: str) -> float:
     """Parse a printed convergence string into decimal degrees.
 
     ``"+01 54 40.49"`` -> 1 + 54/60 + 40.49/3600 = 1.911247222...
 
     Sixty-three anchors carry one of these, so they are parsed rather than
     transcribed a second time as decimals; the parser is pinned in
     tests/test_projection_engines.py against hand-derived values covering a
     positive angle, a negative one, and beta NCAT's signed zero, and against
     the failure that motivates the explicit sign handling: ``float("-00")`` is
     ``-0.0``, but ``-0.0 + 22/60`` is POSITIVE, so a parser that folds the sign
     into the degrees term alone gets every negative angle with zero degrees
     wrong - which is four of the anchors here.
     """
     parts = text.split()
     if len(parts) != 3:
         raise ValueError(
             f"{text!r} is not a printed degrees/minutes/seconds triple; "
             f"expected three whitespace-separated fields, got {len(parts)}."

  792: # --------------------------------------------------------------------------
  793: # The INVERSE side's derivative. Every engine, no exemptions.
  794: #
  795: # Until the interim H1+H2 gate there was no derivative check on any inverse at
  796: # all: test_convergence_and_scale_agree_with_a_finite_difference differentiates
  797: # the FORWARD mapping only. The gate demonstrated what that costs by seeding the
  798: # inverse's B7 denominator 5040 -> 5000 and watching 1,674 tests stay green.
  799: #
  800: # The check here is the composition rule. If ``inverse`` really is the inverse
  801: # of ``forward``, then the Jacobian of one is the matrix inverse of the other's
  802: # at the same point, so their product is the identity:
  803: #
  804: #     J_inv = [[d phi / dN, d phi / dE],      J_fwd = [[dN / d phi, dN / d lam],
  805: #              [d lam / dN, d lam / dE]]               [dE / d phi, dE / d lam]]
  806: #
  807: #     J_inv . J_fwd = I
  808: #
  809: # Both are taken by central difference on the real public entry points, so no
  810: # engine internals are touched and the test reads the same for all four
  811: # projections. The product is dimensionless, which is what lets one tolerance
  812: # cover engines whose coordinates are metres and whose positions are degrees.
  813: #
  814: # **All four entries are asserted separately.** That is the same lesson the
  815: # closure table above carries: collapsing them with max() lets the entry with
  816: # the larger legitimate truncation hide a defect in another.
  817: # --------------------------------------------------------------------------
  818: 
  819: JACOBIAN_FORWARD_STEP_DEG = 1e-4
  820: JACOBIAN_INVERSE_STEP_M = 10.0
  821: """Central-difference steps, chosen where truncation and round-off cross.
  822: 
  823: For the forward step: truncation goes as h^2/6 times the third derivative,
  824: about 5e-13 relative at 1e-4 degrees; round-off goes as the ulp of a
  825: million-metre coordinate divided by 2h, about 1e-11 relative. For the inverse
  826: step: the same two terms at 10 m give about 4e-13 and 6e-11. Both are
  827: round-off-dominated, and both are near the minimum - measured on an
  828: exact-inverse engine (LC1 261017, 7.8 degrees off its meridian), the worst
  829: product entry is 1.0e-10 at (1e-3, 100 m), 6.0e-11 at these steps, and
  830: 1.1e-09 at (1e-5, 1 m), so a ten-times-smaller step is ten times WORSE.
  831: """
  832: 
  833: JACOBIAN_TOLERANCE = 5e-9
  834: """How far a product entry may sit from its pinned value.
  835: 
  836: Derived from the finite-difference noise above, not fitted: the worst entry
  837: measured on any engine whose inverse is exact - both Lamberts and the oblique
  838: Mercator, at both probes - is 1.04e-10, so this is about fifty times the
  839: measured noise floor. It is deliberately ONE absolute number for every entry of
  840: every engine, so that a pinned truncation value and a pinned zero are held to
  841: the same standard and no engine gets a tolerance of its own.
  842: """
  843:

  847:     #
  848:     # Zero means "identity to within the finite-difference noise": the engine's
  849:     # inverse is exact there, and the pinned zero says so. A non-zero value is
  850:     # the engine's own legitimate series truncation, measured.
  851:     #

  861:     # The transverse Mercator is the one engine whose inverse is a truncated

  863:     # d(lat)/dN . dN/d(lat) - 1 = +4.7e-10 (inside the noise, pinned 0),
  864:     # the two cross terms +1.062611e-07 and +2.655635e-09, and
  865:     # d(lon)/dE . dE/d(lon) - 1 = -2.193424e-08.
  866:     #
  867:     # The last of those is what the gate's B7 seed moves: 5040 -> 5000 takes it
  868:     # to -4.366964e-08, a shift of 2.17e-08, more than four times this
  869:     # tolerance. The cross term +1.062611e-07 does NOT move, which is why the
  870:     # entries are pinned one by one.
  871:     ("261002", 40.2, 7.8, (0.0, 1.062611e-07, 2.655635e-09, -2.193424e-08)),
  872: )

  875: def _jacobian_forward(latitude, longitude, zone):
  876:     """[[dN/dphi, dN/dlam], [dE/dphi, dE/dlam]], metres per degree."""
  877:     step = JACOBIAN_FORWARD_STEP_DEG
  878:     north = projection.forward(latitude + step, longitude, zone)
  879:     south = projection.forward(latitude - step, longitude, zone)
  880:     east = projection.forward(latitude, longitude + step, zone)
  881:     west = projection.forward(latitude, longitude - step, zone)
  882:     return (
  883:         (north.northing - south.northing) / (2.0 * step),
  884:         (east.northing - west.northing) / (2.0 * step),
  885:         (north.easting - south.easting) / (2.0 * step),
  886:         (east.easting - west.easting) / (2.0 * step),
  887:     )
  888: 
  889: 
  890: def _jacobian_inverse(northing, easting, zone):
  891:     """[[dphi/dN, dphi/dE], [dlam/dN, dlam/dE]], degrees per metre."""
  892:     step = JACOBIAN_INVERSE_STEP_M
  893:     up = projection.inverse(northing + step, easting, zone)
  894:     down = projection.inverse(northing - step, easting, zone)
  895:     right = projection.inverse(northing, easting + step, zone)
  896:     left = projection.inverse(northing, easting - step, zone)
  897:     return (
  898:         (up.latitude - down.latitude) / (2.0 * step),
  899:         (right.latitude - left.latitude) / (2.0 * step),
  900:         (up.longitude - down.longitude) / (2.0 * step),
  901:         (right.longitude - left.longitude) / (2.0 * step),
  902:     )
  903: 
  904: 
  905: def _jacobian_product_minus_identity(latitude, longitude, zone):
  906:     """J_inv . J_fwd - I, as four numbers in reading order."""
  907:     point = projection.forward(latitude, longitude, zone)
  908:     f11, f12, f21, f22 = _jacobian_forward(latitude, longitude, zone)
  909:     g11, g12, g21, g22 = _jacobian_inverse(point.northing, point.easting, zone)
  910:     return (
  911:         g11 * f11 + g12 * f21 - 1.0,
  912:         g11 * f12 + g12 * f22,
  913:         g21 * f11 + g22 * f21,
  914:         g21 * f12 + g22 * f22 - 1.0,
  915:     )

  924:     code, latitude, offset, expected
  925: ):
  926:     """The inverse's derivative, checked against the forward's, entry by entry.
  927: 
  928:     A round trip composes the two mappings and can hide a defect inside a
  929:     legitimate truncation; this composes their DERIVATIVES, where a high-order
  930:     coefficient's contribution is amplified by its own order and cannot be
  931:     absorbed by the other coordinate's residual, because each entry is asserted
  932:     on its own.
  933: 
  934:     Both probes matter and they say different things. In the zone, every entry
  935:     of every engine must be at the finite-difference noise floor - there is no
  936:     truncation to hide behind, so this is a flat statement that each inverse is
  937:     the inverse. Far out, the exact engines must STILL be at the floor, and the
  938:     one truncated engine must match its measured curve.
  939:     """
  940:     zone = zone_by_code(code)
  941:     longitude = zone.definition.lon_origin - offset
  942: 
  943:     measured = _jacobian_product_minus_identity(latitude, longitude, zone)
  944: 
  945:     names = ("d(lat)/dN.dN/d(lat)-1", "d(lat)/dE.dE/d(lat)", "d(lon)/dN.dN/d(lon)", "d(lon)/dE.dE/d(lon)-1")

  175: SPCS2022_PRINTED = {
  176:     # Beta NCAT prints linear values to 0.001, in metres and in international
  177:     # feet alike. A figure printed to three decimals carries +/-0.0005 of
  178:     # quantization on its own, so that is the tightest a printed figure can be
  179:     # held to and it is what these anchors are held to. (The SPCS 83 anchors in
  180:     # ncat_anchors.py allow 0.001 m, a little headroom above the same floor;
  181:     # this is the stricter choice, and the measured worst case across all 63
  182:     # anchors is 4.994e-4 m - inside the floor, which is what agreement to
  183:     # better than the printed precision looks like.)
  184:     "linear_m": 0.0005,
  185:     "linear_ift": 0.0005,
  186:     # Convergence is printed to 0.01 arc second; half a unit there is 0.005.
  187:     "convergence_arcsec": 0.005,
  188:     # The grid scale factor is printed to nine decimal places, so the
  189:     # quantization interval is 1e-9 and a printed figure can be held to HALF of
  190:     # that - 5e-10 - and no looser. An earlier draft allowed a full 1e-9, which
  191:     # is twice the limit the printed precision supports: the interim H1+H2 gate
  192:     # showed that at that tolerance an engine result of 0.99985823075 passes
  193:     # against NGS's printed 0.999858230 even though it prints as 0.999858231,
  194:     # i.e. a value that DISAGREES with NGS at NGS's own precision. Tightened to
  195:     # the half-quantum bound.
  196:     #
  197:     # Measured worst across all 63 anchors: 4.9673e-10, at zone 261006's
  198:     # +0.15/+0.25 point - inside the bound by 0.65%, which is close and is
  199:     # EXPECTED to be close rather than lucky. NGS's printed 1.000034419 is the
  200:     # rounding of a true value near ...4185, and this engine computes
  201:     # 1.000034418503; a value sitting almost exactly on a rounding boundary
  202:     # necessarily shows a deviation approaching half a quantum, and cannot
  203:     # exceed it while still printing the same string. Four of the 63 sit above
  204:     # 4.9e-10 for that reason, none above 5e-10, and all 63 print IDENTICALLY
  205:     # to NGS at nine decimals - which is the statement this tolerance exists to
  206:     # make.
  207:     "scale_factor": 5e-10,
  208: }
  209: """Tolerances, each derived from the precision beta NCAT printed - never chosen
  210: to make a test pass. A printed figure cannot be held to more than half a unit in
  211: its last place, and holding it to less would let a real error hide."""
